question.text: Scenario: Mrs. Kavita is 50 years old and plans to retire at 60. She currently earns Rs. 1,50,000 per month and has accumulated Rs. 45 lakh in various retirement-linked investments (EPF: Rs. 20 lakh, PPF: Rs. 10 lakh, NPS: Rs. 15 lakh). Her monthly expenses are Rs. 70,000 (of which Rs. 8,000 is healthcare). She estimates needing Rs. 65,000 per month in today's terms at retirement (reduced due to paid-off home loan). General inflation is 6%, healthcare inflation is 10%, and her pre-retirement portfolio return is 9%. Post-retirement, she expects a 7% nominal return. Her life expectancy is 82 years. Three years ago, she withdrew Rs. 2,00,000 from her EPF for a family emergency. She is considering a step-up SIP strategy for the remaining 10 years and is evaluating whether to invest in an annuity or a systematic withdrawal plan (SWP) at retirement. Question 5 of 5: At retirement, Mrs. Kavita will be 60 with a life expectancy of 82 (22 years in retirement). She is evaluating retirement products. Based on the NISM curriculum's criteria for the retirement phase (around retirement age), which combination of evaluation criteria and product recommendations is MOST appropriate?

answer.text: Criteria: Cost, return, and risk tolerance; Products: Continue 100% in equity mutual funds and NPS for maximum growth
Criteria: Liquidity for heirs and capital protection; Products: 100% in bank fixed deposits and savings accounts

Criteria: Inflation protection, capital protection, and income generation; Products: A mix of SCSS, annuity/SWP for guaranteed income, debt/fixed-income products, and balanced/hybrid funds for moderate growth
Criteria: Tax efficiency and high returns; Products: 100% in NPS Tier-I and ELSS funds for tax savings

explanation.text: The Logic: For the retirement phase (at or around retirement age), the NISM X-B workbook specifies three key evaluation criteria: inflation protection, capital protection, and income generation. The product mix should balance guaranteed income (SCSS, annuity, SWP) with moderate growth to beat inflation (balanced/hybrid funds, debt products). 100% equity is too risky, and 100% FDs will not keep pace with inflation over a long retirement. The Trap: Option A applies pre-retirement criteria (cost, return, risk) and suggests 100% equity, which is inappropriate at retirement due to sequence-of-returns risk. Option B applies post-retirement (75+) criteria (liquidity for heirs) prematurely and suggests 100% fixed income, which will lose to inflation over a long retirement. Option D focuses on tax efficiency (a pre-retirement criterion) and suggests products meant for accumulation, not distribution. Cross-Exam Context: NISM X-B categorizes product evaluation criteria into three life stages: pre-retirement (cost, return, risk, tax efficiency), retirement (inflation protection, capital protection, income), and post-retirement 75+ (income, capital protection, liquidity for heirs). Note: PMVVY is no longer available for new investment (PMVVY investments are not available after March 31, 2023, per the X-B workbook), so retirement-income recommendations should rely on SCSS, annuity/SWP, FDs/debt funds, and hybrid funds instead.
